reviewer.role: Critic-style manual historical and pedagogical review
reviewer.independence: Manual review of a human-supplied article; not a runtime Critic 0.1 execution.

checks.note: Institutional and primary-document sources support the Bell Labs transistor chronology, Manchester Baby program, punched and magnetic media distinctions, IBM floppy history, FORTRAN dates, team, IBM 704 target and compiler significance.
A new scope paragraph prevents the FORTRAN-centered narrative from claiming to be an exhaustive catalogue of every candidate for the first programming language.
The public source register uses IBM, IBM Research, University of Manchester, Computer History Museum, Science Museum, the preserved IBM 704 manual and the current Fortran community site.

PRINT, FORMAT, integer I-formatting and the fixed-form column layout are consistent with the preserved IBM 704 FORTRAN manual. The fenced block retains leading spaces; no local gfortran runtime was available and none is claimed.

Questions precede explanations, terms are introduced before reliance, visible state changes anchor the model, and the learner still has to connect the successive abstraction layers. This conforms to the productive-difficulty principle.
The untouched supplied file and its SHA-256 are preserved. Every editorial difference is enumerated in input-provenance.md.
The article contains historical pseudocode and non-destructive examples only; it contains no credentials or unsafe operational instructions.

resolvedIssues.before: The title could imply a complete or singular first-language history.
resolvedIssues.resolution: Added a narrow statement that this is one important development path and not a complete catalogue.

resolvedIssues.before: The supplied copy attached the symbolic-programming claim to the exact year 1947.
resolvedIssues.resolution: Changed the date to the end of the 1940s and described the Birkbeck machine context without overstating a single invention date.

limitations: The article is an educational synthesis, not an exhaustive historiography of all early programming-language candidates.
The reconstructed FORTRAN program is validated as a teaching example in historical style, not asserted to be an archived 1957 card deck.
This review does not claim a Writer 0.1 or runtime Critic 0.1 execution.
